title: Veronica Guerin
full_review:
"Veronica Guerin" (Touchstone) tells the truth-based story of an Irish investigative journalist whose murder in 1996 for exposing high-level organized crime made her a national hero and helped turn the tide of Ireland's war on drugs.

While Guerin's real-life martyrdom makes for compelling drama, the biopic, directed by Joel Schumacher, hedges awkwardly between grittiness and gloss, resulting in a stylistically schizophrenic -- yet ultimately engaging -- portrait of heroism.

Australian actress Cate Blanchett plays slain crusader Veronica Guerin, a fearless, uncompromising reporter whose sense of moral outrage over Dublin's spiraling heroin problem -- which had reached crisis proportions by the early 1990s -- sets her on a collision course with the city's ruthless drug lords. Ostracized by many in the news establishment for her spotty professional pedigree and unconventional style -- dealing face-to-face with informants in pubs and brothels rather than conducting interviews over the phone -- what Guerin lacks in credentials she more than makes up for in moxie and a bullheaded tenacity to score the scoop.

Writing for the country's top-selling paper, The Sunday Independent, Guerin channels her journalistic zeal into blowing the lid off the hydra-like drug gangs whose turf wars had turned Dublin into a combat zone of death and violence. Confident that the pen is mightier than the sword, she embarks on a campaign to effect change by exposing the pushers' brutality, as well as the ineffectiveness of laws that allow the gangs to operate with impunity.

Bucking the system, Guerin starts down a dangerous path, tapping for information contacts on both sides of the law, including a shady underworld braggart named John Traynor (Ciaran Hinds).

Piece by piece Guerin begins to uncover a paper trail of laundered money leading to a brutal kingpin named John Gilligan (Gerard McSorley). Ignoring pleas from family and co-workers fearing for her safety, Guerin persists in pursuing the story, refusing to give in to Gilligan's intimidation tactics.

Braving threats, bullets and beatings, she is sucked deeper by her investigation into a lethal vortex that ends tragically at an intersection on the outskirts of Dublin. There she is gunned down, execution style, by a motorcyclist who pulls up alongside her car stopped at a traffic light. The film ends with a coda showing how her death galvanized the anti-drug forces in Ireland and acted as a catalyst to bolster the country's criminal laws.

While effectively documenting the dangers faced by Guerin, the film fails to plumb the emotional depths of such a complex character or shed light on why she would risk her life and the safety of her family for a news story. Apart from a smattering of perfunctory scenes of Guerin's domestic life with her husband, Graham (Barry Barnes), and their young son, no attempt is made to open a window into her soul. Her character seems bereft of inner conflict. The film keeps Guerin at arm's length, content to observe her heroism without ever really trying to understand it.

Because of the filmmaker's refusal to plunge into deeper psychological waters, Guerin, as depicted, comes across at times as reckless and her bold defiance is tinged with a scent of foolhardiness. Throughout the film her husband's concerns are met with replies extolling self-fulfillment above personal safety -- with little mention given to her maternal responsibilities. Without any insights into what makes her tick, these responses seem myopically cavalier, if not selfish -- leaving viewers with the sense that her single-minded dedication, no matter how just the cause, is driven as much by ego and obstinacy as it is by passion.

The story also is not well-served by the filmmaker employing visuals and music that seem to cue the audience to the desired emotional response. Such manipulative attempts to manufacture emotion, rather than trusting in the narrative's inherent drama, diminish the film's overall cathartic impact. While reigning in their usual blockbuster banality, Schumacher and producer Jerry Bruckheimer -- whose resumes include such social realism classics as "Batman Forever" and "Bad Boys" -- seem ill-fitted for the project, at times eschewing the grittiness the film demands for slicked-up superficiality.

No amount of Hollywood evisceration, however, can strip the story of its ability to inspire and edify. "Veronica Guerin," despite its flaws, is a powerful testimony of courage and personal sacrifice, which eloquently illustrates the Christian calling to "hunger and thirst for justice" -- even at the cost of one's life.

Due to recurring graphic violence and drug abuse, an implied sexual encounter, as well as much rough and crude language and profanity, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
